```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%",

                        if (isTRUE(capabilities("cairo"))) "svg" else "png")
library(Rcausality)
options(width = 110)
# Long-running results are precomputed and shipped in vignettes/precomputed/;
# the code shown is exactly the code that produced them.
# Sys.setenv(RCAUSALITY_RECOMPUTE = "true") recomputes everything.
.pre <- function(name, expr) {
  f <- file.path("precomputed", paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (file.exists(f) && !identical(Sys.getenv("RCAUSALITY_RECOMPUTE"), "true")) return(readRDS(f))
  v <- expr
  dir.create("precomputed", showWarnings = FALSE)
  saveRDS(v, f, compress = "xz")
  v
}
has_ranger <- requireNamespace("ranger", quietly = TRUE)
```

# Overview

Two questions go beyond the analysis of a handful of long time series.

*Panel data.* The same variables are observed in many units -- countries,
sectors, firms, subjects -- often for a few periods only. No unit is long
enough for a reliable test, the units differ, and a link may exist in some
of them only.

*One explained variable.* The interest is in one target: which of the
other variables drive it, at which lag, how strongly, directly or through
another variable -- and how the explanatory variables drive each other.

Both analyses use the methods of `rcausality()`, with the same three
options in every call:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `method` | the causality method (`causal_methods()` lists them) |
| `bayes` | `TRUE` for the Bayesian variant of the method |
| `cores` | number of CPU cores; the results do not depend on it |

and two arguments that set the task:

| Task | Call | Result |
|---|---|---|
| time series | `rcausality(x)` | `causres` |
| panel data | `rcausality(x, id = , time = )` or `panel_causality()` | `causpanel` |
| drivers of a target | `rcausality(x, target = )` or `causal_drivers()` | `causdrivers` |
| drivers of a target in a panel | `causal_drivers(x, target = , id = , time = )` | both |

The panel and the target analysis generalise the Granger-based procedures
of Kosztyán, Mátrai and Kiss (2026) -- unit-by-unit tests with
false-discovery-rate control next to pooled tests, traditional, Bayesian and
random-forest variants, placebo checks, and the explanatory analysis of one
dependent variable -- to all methods of the package.

# One interface for all methods

```{r methods}
causal_methods()[, c("method", "type", "conditional", "pooled", "min_length")]
```

`type` tells whether the method assumes a linear model, `conditional`
whether it can condition on the other series, `pooled` whether it has a
pooled estimator for short panels, and `min_length` the series length from
which the method is advisable for a single series. The settings of a method
are shown by `causal_methods("te")` and passed in `method_args`:

```{r oneif, eval = FALSE}
d <- sim_logistic(300, "x_to_y", seed = 1)
rcausality(d, method = "te", method_args = list(bins = 6))     # a method setting
rcausality(d, method = "te", bayes = TRUE)                     # the Bayesian variant
rcausality(d, method = "te", bayes = TRUE, cores = 4)          # in parallel
```

# Panel data

## The data

Panel data are given in long format: one row per unit and period, a column
with the unit and (optionally) a column with the period. `panel_long()`
converts `time x unit` matrices and `variable x unit x time` arrays.

```{r data}
pd <- sim_panel(n_units = 30, n_time = 25, scenario = "x_to_y", prevalence = 0.6,
                coupling = 0.5, seed = 1)
head(pd, 3)
```

`sim_panel()` simulates 30 units observed for 25 periods. `x` drives `y`
in 60% of the units only (`prevalence`), with a strength that differs from
unit to unit; every unit has its own level (fixed effects).

## Three levels of evidence

```{r panel}
pg <- rcausality(pd, id = "unit", time = "time", seed = 1)
pg
```

Every directed link is analysed at three levels.

* **Units.** The method is applied to every unit that is long enough for
  it. `11/30 (9)` reads: the link is found in 11 of the 30 units at the 5%
  level, in 9 of them after the Benjamini-Hochberg correction over all unit
  x link cells.
* **Group.** One test of "no unit has the link", built from the unit
  results: the unit statistics are standardised with their own null
  distributions and added up. It is sensitive to a link in *some* units, of
  any sign.
* **Pooled.** One estimate from all units together. It is sensitive to an
  effect that has the same direction in most units, and it is available
  also when the units are too short to be analysed one by one.

By default the panel decision uses both levels (`panel_control(decision =
)`): the smaller of the two p-values, doubled, and corrected over the links
(`adjust`). The `prevalence` column estimates the share of the units with
the link (posterior mean and credible interval of a model on the unit
Bayes factors); the simulated share is 0.6.

```{r heat, fig.height = 2.9, fig.cap = "Heat map of a panel analysis. Rows: links; columns: units and the two panel-level tests. A coloured cell is a link in that unit (the colour shows the strength of the evidence, or the lag when the lags differ), a star marks the cells that remain after the false-discovery-rate correction."}
plot(pg)
```

```{r units, fig.height = 3.3, fig.cap = "The evidence of every unit for the two links, sorted. A panel-level link can be carried by many units or by a few."}
plot(pg, "units")
```

`plot(pg, "prevalence")` shows the shares, `plot(pg, "network")` the
causal graph of the panel; `summary(pg)` and `pg$panel$detail` give the
details of the tests, `pg$units` the unit table.

## Where the null distributions come from

For the Granger family (`"granger"`, `"bayes_granger"`,
`"toda_yamamoto"`) the panel tests are the following.

* The pooled test is the test of Juodis, Karavias and Sarafidis (2021).
  Under the null hypothesis the coefficients of the cause's lags are zero in
  every unit, so they can be pooled although the units differ; the
  intercept, the own lags of the effect and the lags of the controls keep
  unit-specific coefficients. A pooled estimator of a dynamic model has a
  bias of order `1/T` (Nickell 1981). In the test of the *reverse*
  direction of a true link this bias is the same in all units and
  accumulates: the test rejects a true null hypothesis more and more often
  as the number of units grows. The half-panel jackknife of Dhaene and
  Jochmans (2015) removes the bias.
* In short series the F distribution is only an approximation, because the
  regressors are lagged values of persistent series. The unit statistics and
  the pooled statistic are therefore compared with a bootstrap under the
  null hypothesis, as Dumitrescu and Hurlin (2012) recommend for their panel
  test: in every unit the effect is regenerated from its own estimated
  autoregression with resampled residuals, the cause is kept. The bootstrap
  sample is the null sample of the group test, and it calibrates the unit
  p-values and the pooled p-value (an *empirical null*, Efron 2004); the
  calibration can only make a test more conservative.

The following experiment shows why this matters. The null hypothesis is
true in every case; a test at the 5% level should reject in 5% of the
panels. The table gives the rejection rates of the classical tests -- the
Dumitrescu-Hurlin statistic with its normal approximation and the
fixed-effects F-test with common coefficients -- and of the tests of the
package.

```{r size, echo = FALSE}
size_tab <- .pre("panel-size", {
  ns <- asNamespace("Rcausality")
  one <- function(s, N, T, sc, ar) {
    p <- sim_panel(n_units = N, n_time = T, scenario = sc, ar = ar, seed = s)
    a <- rcausality(p, id = "unit", time = "time", lag = 1, seed = s, adjust = "none")
    P <- a$panel[a$panel$cause == "y", ]                          # y -> x: no such link in any scenario
    dh <- rcausality(p, id = "unit", time = "time", lag = 1, seed = s, adjust = "none",
                     panel = panel_control(levels = c("units", "group"), combine = "dh"))$panel
    U <- ns$.panel_units(p, "unit", "time")$units
    fe <- ns$.pooled_F(ns$.panel_design(U, "x", "y", character(0), 1L))$p_value
    c(dh = dh$p_freq[dh$cause == "y"] < 0.05, fe = fe < 0.05, group = P$p_freq[P$level == "group"] < 0.05,
      pooled = P$p_freq[P$level == "pooled"] < 0.05, both = a$pairs$p_value[a$pairs$cause == "y"] < 0.05)
  }
  cfg <- list(list("independent series, AR coefficient 0.5", 30, 20, "independent", 0.5),
              list("independent series, AR coefficient 0.8", 30, 20, "independent", 0.8),
              list("reverse direction of a true link, 30 units", 30, 20, "x_to_y", 0.5),
              list("reverse direction of a true link, 100 units", 100, 20, "x_to_y", 0.5))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(cfg, function(g) {
    r <- rowMeans(vapply(seq_len(200), function(s) one(s, g[[2]], g[[3]], g[[4]], g[[5]]), numeric(5)))
    data.frame(panel = g[[1]], units = g[[2]], periods = g[[3]], t(100 * r), check.names = FALSE)
  }))
})
knitr::kable(size_tab, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Panel (the null hypothesis is true)", "Units", "Periods", "Dumitrescu-Hurlin, asymptotic",
                           "Fixed-effects F-test", "Group", "Pooled", "Group or pooled"),
             caption = "Rejection rates (%) of tests at the 5% level when the null hypothesis is true; 200 simulated panels per row, lag order 1.")
```

The Dumitrescu-Hurlin test with its normal approximation is far from its
nominal level in short panels, the more so the more persistent the series
are, and the fixed-effects test of the reverse direction rejects a true
null hypothesis in almost half of the wide panels. The tests of the package
stay between 2.5% and 8%.

For the model-free methods the pooled statistic is computed from the
stacked delay vectors of all units, standardised within the units, and its
null distribution from surrogate panels in which the cause is delayed
circularly within every unit. In short units a shifted series is not
independent of the original one, which makes these tests conservative.
The units are treated as independent throughout; with common shocks,
`panel_control(time_effects = TRUE)` centres every variable across the
units within each period first.

## Choosing the method

The method is an option, as for time series. In the next panel `x` acts
on `y` through its square, a dependence that leaves no linear trace; the
units have 20 periods.

```{r nonlinear}
pn <- sim_panel(n_units = 40, n_time = 20, scenario = "x_to_y", nonlinear = TRUE,
                coupling = 0.5, heterogeneity = 0.2, seed = 1)
cmp <- .pre("panel-compare",
            compare_methods(pn, methods = c("granger", "cmi", "rf_granger"),
                            id = "unit", time = "time", n_perm = 200, seed = 1, cores = 2))
cmp
sapply(cmp$results, function(r) r$pairs$p_adj[r$pairs$cause == "x"])   # adjusted p-values of x -> y
```

The linear test finds nothing; the conditional mutual information and the
random forest find `x -> y`. Units of 20 periods are too short for a kNN
estimate of the conditional mutual information or for a random forest, so
these two methods are run at the pooled level only, where the delay vectors
of all 40 units are used together.

## The Bayesian variants

`bayes = TRUE` gives the Bayesian variant of the panel analysis of every
method.

```{r bayes}
pb <- rcausality(pd, id = "unit", time = "time", bayes = TRUE, prior = "hyper_g", seed = 1)
pb
```

* **Units**: the Bayes factors of the method (`prior`, see
  `bayes_control()`). A prevalence model combines them: the share of the
  units with the link has a Beta prior, which gives the posterior of the
  share and, for every unit, a posterior probability of the link that
  borrows strength from the panel (`pb$units$post_pooled`). The units are
  selected by the Bayesian false discovery rate.
* **Group**: the Bayes factor of the group statistic against its null
  distribution.
* **Pooled**: for the Granger family the Bayes factor of the pooled
  estimate under the chosen prior (BIC, g, hyper-g, normal / spike-and-slab,
  Minnesota); for the model-free methods the Bayes factor of the pooled
  statistic against its surrogates (`surrogate_bf()`).

The panel decision averages the two Bayes factors, which is the Bayes
factor of "a link at one of the two levels".

# The causal drivers of one variable

## Time series

`sim_drivers()` simulates five series: `x1` drives `y` at lag 1, `x3`
drives `y` at lag 2, `x2` drives `x1` -- and therefore `y`, but only
through `x1` -- and `x4` is unrelated noise.

```{r drivers}
d <- sim_drivers(300, seed = 1)
cd <- causal_drivers(d, target = "y")
cd
```

The analysis tests three families of links and corrects each of them for
multiplicity separately: the links into the target, the links from the
target (feedback) and the links among the explanatory variables.

* `importance` is the share of a driver in the evidence for the links into
  the target.
* `direct`: for the methods that can condition on other series, every
  driver is tested again given all other series. `x2` is a driver of `y`,
  but not given `x1`: it is an *indirect* driver, and `via` names the
  mediator, a direct driver that `x2` drives.
* `lag` is the delay at which the driver acts most strongly, `order` the
  lag order of the Granger test (by default the first significant order,
  as in the lag ladder of Kosztyán, Mátrai and Kiss 2026). The two differ
  for `x3`: its effect sits at lag 2, but the first lag of an autocorrelated
  series is a proxy of its second lag, so the order-1 test is already
  significant.

```{r ladder, fig.height = 4.8, fig.cap = "The lag ladder. The target stands on the right; every driver is placed in the column of its lag, from top to bottom by importance. Solid arrows are direct links, dashed arrows links that vanish given the other series; the bar in a box is the importance; the thin arrows are the links among the explanatory variables."}
plot(cd)
```

```{r importance, fig.height = 3, fig.cap = "Importance of the explanatory variables with their evidence, lag and role."}
plot(cd, "importance")
```

`cd$drivers` holds the table, `cd$graph` the links among the explanatory
variables, `plot(cd, "graph")` draws the causal network of all series.
The same analysis runs with every method and its Bayesian variant:

```{r drivers-cmi}
ct <- .pre("drivers-cmi",
           causal_drivers(d, target = "y", method = "cmi", bayes = TRUE, max_lag = 3,
                          n_perm = 200, seed = 1, cores = 2))
ct$drivers[, c("driver", "lag", "bf10", "significant", "importance", "direct", "role")]
```

The conditional mutual information finds the two direct drivers with their
lags; the evidence for the indirect driver `x2` stays below the threshold
of the Bayes factor.

## Panels

With `id` the drivers are those of the panel; the explanatory graph and
the direct / indirect distinction are derived from the panel-level tests.

```{r pdrivers}
pdd <- sim_panel(n_units = 30, n_time = 30, scenario = "drivers", coupling = 0.5, seed = 1)
cp <- .pre("panel-drivers",
           causal_drivers(pdd, target = "y", id = "unit", time = "time", seed = 1))
cp
```

```{r pheat, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "The drivers of the target in every unit and in the panel."}
plot(cp, "heatmap")
```

`plot(cp)` draws the lag ladder of the panel.

# Are the links robust?

`placebo_test()` and `robustness()` accept panel and target analyses.
A placebo panel reassigns every variable across the units -- each unit
gets its `x` and its `y` from two different units -- which keeps the
dynamics of every series and removes the links; the whole analysis is
repeated on every placebo panel. The robustness check repeats the analysis
with other lag orders, other corrections, random subsets of the units and
other methods, and reports the decision of each panel level.

```{r robust}
pl <- .pre("panel-placebo", placebo_test(pg, n_placebo = 49, seed = 1, cores = 2))
pl
rb <- .pre("panel-robust",
           robustness(pg, lags = 1:2, n_sub = 10, methods = "toda_yamamoto", seed = 1, cores = 2))
rb
```

# Do the links help to forecast?

`predict()` turns the links of the panel into forecast equations that are
pooled over the units (unit fixed effects and unit scales, common
coefficients) and compares them with the own-lags model on the last periods
of every unit; `forecast_compare()` does this for several causality methods,
with the links selected on the training periods only.

```{r forecast, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "Left: hold-out improvement of the causal model over the own-lags model by unit. Other panels: observed series, one-step hold-out predictions and forecasts for three units."}
fc <- predict(pg, h = 4)
fc
plot(fc, units = c("u01", "u02", "u03"))
```

```{r fcmp}
.pre("panel-fcmp",
     forecast_compare(pd, methods = c("granger", "toda_yamamoto"), id = "unit", time = "time", seed = 1))
```

# Parallel computing

The units, the links, the bootstrap and surrogate samples and the placebo
runs are distributed over the cores; every unit of work has its own random
stream, so the results are identical for any number of cores.

```{r cores, eval = FALSE}
options(Rcausality.cores = 4)                         # for the session
rcausality(pd, id = "unit", time = "time", method = "cmi", cores = 4, seed = 1)
```
